markscheme_points.text: emission of particles/radiation by unstable nucleus

hints: Hint 1: Think about what is actually unstable here - it is the nucleus itself, not the whole atom, and what must it do to become more stable?
Hint 2: Think about whether anything needs to trigger this change from outside, or whether it happens entirely on its own at random.
parts.proper_answer: Radioactive decay is the spontaneous disintegration of an unstable nucleus with the emission of particles and/or electromagnetic radiation.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What is decaying?**
Think of a nucleus that has the wrong balance of protons and neutrons. It has too much energy to stay as it is, so it rearranges itself to a more stable form by throwing out mass-energy as alpha, beta or gamma radiation.

Step 2: **Why is it spontaneous?**
This happens randomly and spontaneously. Spontaneous means it is not triggered by any outside influence like temperature, pressure or chemical bonding. You cannot predict when one nucleus will decay, only the probability for a large number.

markscheme_points.text: use of graph to determine half-life = 14 minutes
N at 14 minutes = 4.4 × 10⁷ and A = λN
correct tangent drawn at time t = 14 minutes
magnitude of gradient of tangent identified as activity
correct working for gradient leading to activity

hints: Hint 1: Remember that activity $A$ is the rate of decay, so $A = -\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta t}$. On an $N$ against $t$ graph this is the magnitude of the gradient. Alternatively $A = \lambda N$, so you will need $\lambda$ and $N$.
Hint 2: Look at Fig. 13.1 to find the half-life $T_{1/2}$. Start from $N_0 \approx 8.8 \times 10^7$ at $t = 0$ and see when $N$ falls to half that value.
Hint 3: Read the value of $N$ at $t = 14.0$ min from the graph and convert the half-life from minutes to seconds, since activity in $\text{Bq}$ means decays per second.
Hint 4: Combine your values using $\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$ and $A = \lambda N$ at $t = 14.0$ min to get $A$ in $\text{Bq}$.
parts.proper_answer: Half-life $T_{1/2} \approx 14$ min, $N$ at 14 min $\approx 4.4 \times 10^7$. $A = \lambda N = \frac{\ln 2}{14 \times 60} \times 4.4 \times 10^7 \approx 3.6 \times 10^4\text{ Bq}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link activity to the graph**
Activity is the number of decays per second: $$A = -\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$$ So you can either draw a tangent at $t = 14.0$ min and find its gradient, or find $\lambda$ from the half-life and multiply by $N$. The half-life route is usually more accurate here.

Step 2: **Find the half-life from Fig. 13.1**
At $t = 0$, $N_0 \approx 8.8 \times 10^7$. Half of this is: $$\frac{N_0}{2} \approx 4.4 \times 10^7$$ From the graph, $N = 4.4 \times 10^7$ occurs at: $$t \approx 14 \text{ min}$$ So $T_{1/2} \approx 14$ min. This is also the time you are asked about, which makes the calculation neat.

Step 3: **Get $\lambda$ and $N$ in SI units**
Convert half-life to seconds: $$T_{1/2} = 14 \times 60 = 840\text{ s}$$ Then: $$\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{840}$$ At $t = 14.0$ min, read directly from the curve: $$N \approx 4.4 \times 10^7$$

Step 4: **Calculate activity**
Now use $A = \lambda N$: $$A = \frac{0.693}{14 \times 60} \times 4.4 \times 10^7$$ $$A \approx 3.6 \times 10^4\text{ Bq}$$ This is decays per second, so the unit $\text{Bq}$ is correct. A tangent gradient at 14 min gives the same result within experimental uncertainty.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: You are told not to use the half-life. Focus on the direct link between the activity you just found and the number of nuclei present at that same instant: $A = \lambda N$.
Hint 2: Read $N$ at $t = 14.0$ min from Fig. 13.1 again, keep $A$ in $\text{Bq}$ (per second), and rearrange to $\lambda = A/N$ to get $\lambda$ in $\text{s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use $A = \lambda N$ directly**
At any instant, activity and number of undecayed nuclei are proportional: $$A = \lambda N$$ So the decay constant is: $$\lambda = \frac{A}{N}$$ You already have $A$ at 14.0 min from (i), and $N$ at the same time from the graph.

Step 2: **Substitute values**
Using $A \approx 3.6 \times 10^4\text{ Bq}$ and $N \approx 4.4 \times 10^7$: $$\lambda = \frac{3.6 \times 10^4}{4.4 \times 10^7}$$ $$\lambda \approx 8.2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}^{-1}$$ No half-life needed. Note the unit is per second because $A$ is per second.
